summary: The article explores how ethnobotany, the study of the relationship between people and plants, shapes regional cuisine by reviving native plants and herbs in cooking. It draws on a series of dated statements from chefs, farmers, an environmentalist, a dietitian, an anthropologist and an educator, covering flavor, local economy, conservation, health, culture, innovation and education. It concludes that eating locally connects health, heritage and environment.
one_line: An overview of how ethnobotany and native plants are reviving regional cuisine, supporting local economies, sustainability, health, culture, innovation and education.
key_facts: Ethnobotany is the study of the relationship between people and plants, and it shapes local cuisines and promotes sustainable farming practices.

Chef Marcus O'Reilly of the farm-to-table restaurant Thyme and Tradition spoke on October 15, 2023, saying 'Using native plants is about telling a story, every dish is an ode to history, the land, and its people.'
The Ethnobotanical Farmers' Alliance, headed by Sarah Mendez, published a report on November 17, 2023, on the positive impact of local ingredient use on small-scale farmers and the food economy.
The Global Ethnobotanical Initiative, spearheaded by environmentalist Dr. Leo Carver, highlighted the role of local plants in ecological balance on December 2, 2023.
Dr. Leo Carver states native plants require fewer resources to thrive and help preserve soil health and support local wildlife.
Registered Dietitian Louise Tran released a study on January 20, 2024, revealing antioxidant properties of regional herbs like sagebrush and immune-boosting benefits of wild berries.
Louise Tran says nutrients in local ingredients are sometimes lost in mass-produced crops due to soil depletion and longdistance transportation.
Cultural anthropologist Dr. Maya Peterson discussed on February 14, 2024, how culinary traditions maintain cultural heritage, calling native ingredients 'the lexicon of this language.'
Chef Javier Gomez, known for using Amazonian herbs in avant-garde dishes, appeared at the International Culinary Arts Symposium on March 5, 2024.
The Harvest Heritage Program, led by educator Alice Nguyen, launched on April 22, 2024, and integrates garden-based learning with cultural studies in schools.
The article dates the modern culinary renaissance's emphasis on traditional flavors to around September 1, 2023.
Native ingredients are being rediscovered in places from Mexico City to the countryside of Tuscany.
